text:
Today i ll present the refinement of my msc thesis on graph-structured multi-agent reinforcement learning for power grid topology control and the results of the first baseline i implemented.

The goal is to improve how reinforcement learning can scale and coordinate decisions in realistic power grid environments.”

name: Titre 1
text: Motivation
textPreview: Motivation

name: Espace réservé du numéro de diapositive 4
ZoneTexte 3
text:
Purpose
TSO need fast congestion management under renewable variability and unforeseen events.
Topology actions are attractive because they can reroute flows before using costly redispatch.

Problem Statement: Power grid operation requires:
Real-time decisions under uncertainty
Maintaining safety constraints (line limits, demand balance)
Operating over large, combinatorial action spaces

Limitations of current approaches
Optimization (OPF) is not scalable and too slow
Single-Agent RL: ignores decentralization
textPreview: Purpose | TSO need fast congestion management under renewable variability and unforeseen events. | Topology actions are attractive becaus...

name: ZoneTexte 7
text:
Research Questions:
Does a GNN encoder improve performance vs standard MARL baselines?
Can a Multi agent approach/match single agent approach under partial observability?
Does any improvements generalize to larger grid (bus14 to bus 36)?
Can the agents learn how to behave in a « human operator » way ?
textPreview: Research Questions: | Does a GNN encoder improve performance vs standard MARL baselines? | Can a Multi agent approach/match single agent ...

text:
Power grid operation is a challenging control problem.
Operators need to make real-time decisions under uncertainty, while maintaining strict safety constraints like line limits and supply-demand balance.

One important control mechanism is topology actions, which allow rerouting power flows by modifying the grid structure.

Reinforcement learning is promising for this type of sequential decision-making problem, but the action space is extremely large.

Current approaches have limitations:
- optimization methods are too slow and don’t scale well and they don't enable real time monitoring
- single-agent RL ignores decentralization that is happening in real life
- and existing multi-agent RL still struggles with coordination and scalability.

text: The strongest Grid2Op agents are rarely “pure RL.” They combine learning with action reduction, hierarchy, heuristics, simulation, search, curriculum learning, or safety constraints. Multi-agent topology control is much newer and is still mostly based on hierarchical or centrally coordinated decompositions.

text: “A chronic is a complete time series of load, generation and possible disturbances. I create the train/test split once using a fixed seed. Training workers only access the 80% training subset. During training, I periodically evaluate greedily on held-out chronics and select the best checkpoint using test survival. The final reported performance is computed over the entire held-out split rather than a small sample.”

text: “The grid is partitioned into three strongly connected regions. Each decentralized actor controls only its assigned substations, but its decisions affect the entire grid through the AC power flow. Coordination is therefore implicit: an action that solves a local overload can create congestion in another agent’s region.”

text:
To dive a little deeper i have been looking at a survey that summarize all the algorithms that won the l2rpn challenge and this is the main categories of succesfull agentthat won the challenge.

Some approaches rely on a single global agent with strong engineering tricks.

For example, they use graph neural networks combined with value-based RL, and validate actions using power-flow simulations.

Others reduce the action space using masking or pruning.

These methods can work, so mixing a single agent with rules, but they suffer because the action space remains very large.”

Another important idea is to predict a target topology instead of raw actions.

This is used in SMAAC, where the agent learns an afterstate representation—basically the resulting topology after an action.

This helps because multiple sequences of actions can lead to the same configuration. So it reduces the action space
